ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns, though introductions and presentations shift into long, structured monologues. Early conversation is loose and chatty, with frequent greetings, technical-check questions, joking, and fragmented overlap; speakers often repeat words, restart phrases, and use fillers such as “um,” “yeah,” “okay,” and “you know.” Formality rises for speaker introductions and scientific explanations, but remains warm and conversational rather than polished. Questions are generally indirect and exploratory—often prefaced with praise, disclaimers like “quick question” or “naive question,” and several setup clauses before the actual query. Participants build on one another through affirmations and follow-up questions, while challenges are framed gently as uncertainties or alternative possibilities rather than direct disagreement. Answers are expansive, hedged with phrases like “I think,” “we don’t know,” “it could be,” and “my prediction,” and often acknowledge limitations before offering an interpretation.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Working out why wild bee numbers on farms did not recover after wildflower strips were planted along field edges.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Rahman
speakers.background: A landscape ecologist with 11 years of experience designing and coordinating farm-scale biodiversity monitoring. She has worked with GIS-based landscape metrics, repeated transect and pan-trap surveys, habitat-condition scoring, and spatial sampling designs across mixed arable and livestock systems. She will coordinate field preparation, map field-edge strips and semi-natural habitat, and build the ecological sampling framework.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats the apparent failure of wildflower strips as a scale and resource-continuity problem rather than evidence that strips are ineffective in themselves. She focuses on whether strips are connected to nesting habitat, whether floral resources persist across the season, how surrounding crop composition changes exposure and forage, and whether farm-management information can meaningfully stratify sites before final sampling is fixed. She is comfortable relying on biology for toxicological interpretation and economics for farmer decision-making.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
speakers.background: A pollinator biologist with 14 years of experience in wild-bee community ecology, specimen-based identification, pollen-resource analysis, and pesticide-exposure studies. His laboratory has used residue chemistry, controlled sublethal exposure assays, species-trait databases, and mark-recapture-informed estimates of foraging range. He will lead species identification, exposure-sampling priorities, and interpretation of species-specific responses.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Thomas frames non-recovery as potentially hidden by aggregate bee counts: strips may benefit a few mobile generalists while failing to support oligolectic, short-range, ground-nesting, or pesticide-sensitive taxa. He emphasizes phenology, nesting substrate, floral trait matching, colony and individual-level sublethal effects, and the mismatch between where pesticides are applied and where residues are ultimately encountered. He regards detailed pesticide-use histories from farmers as essential for defensible exposure prioritization.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Maya Ortiz
speakers.background: An agricultural economist and project manager with 8 years of experience supporting evaluations of agri-environment schemes, farm-business surveys, and conservation-payment programs. Her work has included partial-budget analysis, subsidy participation records, crop-yield comparisons, and semi-structured interviews with growers about implementation constraints. She will coordinate the farmer interview workflow and lead analysis of establishment costs, maintenance burdens, payments, yield implications, and income trade-offs.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya sees strip outcomes as inseparable from the practical incentives and constraints that shape establishment and upkeep. She is interested in whether seed mixes, mowing, re-sowing, pesticide practices, and strip placement reflect program rules, cash-flow pressures, labor availability, or perceived yield risk. She is less certain how to connect economic evidence directly to bee-population mechanisms, so she seeks clear ecological and biological guidance on which management details will be analytically meaningful. She notes that the planned farmer interviews, recruitment contact, consent materials, and collection of financial and management information depend on institutional human-participant approval.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: Morning—quick one, did the revised approval form from last week ever come through to everyone? I wanted to use today to pin down the few farm-management questions that are genuinely, genuinely essential, because the interview timeline is getting a bit tight.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: I got the revised form, yes. The essential bits for me are mowing dates and frequency, re-sowing or seed-mix changes, and how the strip edge and the adjacent hedge or bank have been managed. I need those before I freeze the strata, because the six autumn visits already showed very similar-looking strips in completely different nesting contexts.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: Hm, different nesting contexts.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: And I can ask about the hedge or bank, but I'll need it in fairly observable terms, like whether it's cut, sprayed, or bare, that kind of thing. Amina, is strip placement relative to the crop and other flower habitat something you need from the grower, or can you pull most of that from the maps?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Mostly I can use the maps for placement and the wider flower network, and I can do that consistently. What I need from the grower is what the map can't see, whether that bank was cultivated or sprayed, whether a margin was moved, and what was flowering in the crop rotation, especially rape, in the relevant years.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: Could the crop-history question also capture active ingredient, application date, and method for the strip-adjacent fields? I need that history before I can sensibly prioritize residue matrices. The pilot's generalist-dominated cereal-edge site could be exposure, but it could just as readily be- sorry, nesting or phenology.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: Okay, so product name alone won’t be enough. Thomas, if I ask for active ingredient, date, crop, rate, and method just for the adjacent fields, is that your minimum, or do you also need seed treatment history? I’m slightly worried growers won’t have rates to, um, to hand, so I may need to build in a records follow-up rather than make the first interview enormous.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: Seed treatment history is important, particularly for the cereal fields, but I wouldn’t make the first interview depend on getting the rate. If we have the active ingredient or product, whether it was a treated crop or foliar use, the approximate timing, and the application method, I can triage it. Then a records follow-up can get the rates and any repeat applications. We should also ask whether the strip itself, its headland, or the bank was ever directly sprayed.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: Yeah, that gives me a workable first-pass list. I’ll separate the pesticide section into what they can recall in the interview and a records follow-up, including any direct treatment of the strip, headland, or bank; I just need to make sure we don’t contact anyone before the approval clears, since it’s currently expected March 1 even though interviews were pencilled in for February.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Mm, that’s later than expected.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: I saw the form. March 1 means the exposure history will come in pretty close to spring sampling, so I may need to keep the initial residue panel deliberately broad until the records follow-up identifies the plausible active ingredients. I still need to check what the lab can accommodate at the relevant detection limits.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Quick question from last week. Did the candidate-farm boundary file ever get uploaded? I can still map the broad context before March, but I need to check whether we actually have enough, enough contrast in connected banks, bare ground, and semi-natural habitat. Otherwise the management histories may arrive too late to rescue the strata.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: I haven't seen it.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: I think it's in the shared drive, but I'm not sure it's the final boundary file. I'll- I'll check after this, rather than have you map from the wrong version. And just to flag, I can't use those candidate contacts for any recruitment, or even for pre-interview records requests, until the March approval is in.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That's fine on contact. I'm not asking for any outreach before approval. But if the final boundary file can go up this week, I can at least run the landscape and connectivity screen now, and then hold the final strata open for the interview histories, which means...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: Quick question on the boundary file from last week. Will it include field-level adjacency, not just the strip polygons? For exposure, I need to know which cereal or treated crop is actually bordering each strip, because a broad, broad landscape buffer won't distinguish the likely residue pathway.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: I think the final file should have the strip polygons plus the adjacent-field IDs, but I need to verify that. It may only be the farm boundary export. If it’s missing the adjacency layer, can you send me the field-ID format you need, Thomas, so I don’t end up circulating something that still can’t be linked to crop histories?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: If it has a stable farm ID, strip ID, adjacent-field ID, and which side of the strip each field is on, that’s enough to link the histories. Ideally, include the crop for the relevant season too. Otherwise, a treated cereal and, say, a flowering crop can end up in the same adjacency record, which isn’t very useful for interpreting exposure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: For my side, that same adjacency layer is useful even before we have the interview histories, especially if it includes crop by year. I can screen the strips against the surrounding rape blocks and semi-natural features, but I’d rather not treat a flowering crop next door as the same thing as connected nesting habitat. Those were exactly the odd cases in the autumn visits.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: I’ll check whether crop-by-year is actually in the export too, because that sounds like the common minimum instead of two separate asks. If it isn’t, we may need a clean linkage table from whoever supplied the boundaries, though obviously not through the farmers before March, and then—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: And if crop-by-year is missing, I could still use the current-season crop for a provisional screen. I mainly need to see whether the candidate set has enough real variation in nesting connections. Otherwise, we could end up comparing lots of strips that differ in flowers but not in the resource landscape around them.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: Okay, that helps. I’ll treat current-season crop as the fallback for the provisional screen, but I’ll ask the data supplier for the crop-by-year linkage rather than trying to reconstruct it through interviews. For the interviews, the historical rotation can stay focused on the years that matter for the strip and bee- the bee records.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: That works. For the interview, could we still get a rough sense of whether rape was a major part of the rotation around the strip, just yes or no, or approximate years? The map linkage will be better, obviously, but it would help us interpret farms where a big flowering pulse may have pulled activity away from the strip, rather than the strip simply failing.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: I can add that as a light-touch rotation question, whether rape was adjacent or nearby and roughly which years, rather than trying to get acreage estimates on the call. I’ll need to word it clearly so we mean the fields around the strip, not just whether they grow rape somewhere on the holding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Yes, that’s enough for a useful provisional screen.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Thomas Nguyen
transcript.text: Yes, that distinction will matter quite a bit for interpreting the species records.

transcript.speaker: Maya Ortiz
transcript.text: I think I’ll let you both go a few minutes early. I’ll check that boundary- I’ll check the boundary export after this, and we can pick up any gaps next week. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Rahman
transcript.text: Great, speak next week.
